hints: Think carefully about what the question asks: mass of DNA *in a cell*, not in the nucleus. When does one cell actually become two separate cells?
Remember that prophase and anaphase only move chromosomes around inside the same cell, so the total DNA per cell stays doubled until the cytoplasm divides.
walkthrough:
**Recall When DNA Doubles**

Think of the cell cycle like copying a set of instructions. During S phase of interphase, DNA replicates, so the mass of DNA per cell doubles from 2n to 4n.

That doubled amount stays in the one cell as it enters mitosis.

**Check What Mitosis Actually Does**

In prophase the chromosomes condense, and in anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled apart. This is lovely to watch, but it is all still happening inside one cell.

So the mass of DNA in that one cell has not been reduced yet, it has just been rearranged.

**Spot When One Cell Becomes Two**

Cytokinesis is when the cytoplasm divides to form two separate daughter cells. The doubled DNA is now shared out, one complete set per new cell.

That is the moment the mass of DNA *per cell* falls back to the original amount, so the answer is B.

options.A: Anaphase separates sister chromatids to opposite poles, but they are still in one cell, so DNA mass per cell is unchanged.
options.B: Cytokinesis splits one cell into two daughter cells, so each new cell receives half the doubled DNA and the mass per cell is reduced.
options.C: Interphase includes S phase where DNA is replicated, so DNA mass per cell increases (doubles), not reduced.
options.D: Prophase only condenses the already replicated chromosomes inside one cell, so DNA mass per cell stays at the doubled level.
